- Place it on the canvas anchored at the position encoded by the marker pixel's row/col in the bordered square's 3x3 inner grid.

Key insight: The marker pixel's position in a 3x3 grid jointly encodes vertical and horizontal anchor alignment (start/middle/end).

annotation.summary: Use four legend icons on the left to construct a large sprite by combining unit sprite with frame shape, then place it on background at position and rotation indicated by position marker and rotation marker.
annotation.src: unit sprite pattern from legend row 1 s1
annotation.dst: each foreground pixel position in frame shape from legend row 2 d1
annotation.match_cond: s1 replaces each pixel of d1.frame to create enlarged composite sprite
annotation.transform: tile s1 at each d1.pixel position to form fractal-like enlarged sprite
annotation.symbol_instructions: legend row 1: unit sprite pattern; legend row 2: frame shape template; legend row 3: position marker (pixel location in small square indicates anchor on background); legend row 4: rotation indicator (clock-hand style determines rotation angle)
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: read four legend icons from left column; Step 2: construct enlarged sprite by tiling unit sprite into frame shape; Step 3: determine placement position from position marker; Step 4: determine rotation from rotation marker; Step 5: place rotated enlarged sprite at indicated position on background
annotation.src2: the constructed enlarged sprite s2
annotation.dst2: position on main background grid d2
annotation.match_cond2: s2.anchor == position indicated by marker pixel in legend row 3 square; s2.rotation == rotation indicated by clock-hand marker in legend row 4
annotation.transform2: rotate(s2, angle from legend row 4) then place at d2

tags: condition:时钟指针编码角度, clock_hand_encodes_rotation

references.docstring:
Stamp translated copies of a monochrome template guided by a singleton pixel layout.

Input structure:
- bg = background. A large monochrome shape (template, color T).
- Singleton pixels elsewhere: exactly one is color T (layout origin); the rest share color O (overlap color).
- Singletons sit on a uniform-spacing lattice.

Rule:
- Convert each singleton's offset from the origin into coarse lattice units.
- Place a template copy at each offset, scaled by template height/width.
- The origin's copy is painted O instead of T.
- Any pixel covered by two or more copies is also recolored to O.

Key insight: The single T-colored singleton identifies both the origin position and the "self" copy, which is uniquely recolored.

annotation.src: marker pixel set s with different colored center pixel and peripheral pixels
annotation.dst: monochrome sprite d
annotation.match_cond: s.center.color == d.color
annotation.transform: s.peripheral_pixels -> d. d.color -> s.peripheral_pixels.color

references.docstring:
Transmit colored tokens along wire networks, converting each to its complementary 3×3 pattern.

Input structure:
- bg = background. Non-bg cells form wire networks and 3×3 tokens (solid blocks or X/diagonal patterns) near wire endpoints.

Rule:
- Every solid 3×3 token is replaced in-place by a diamond (center + 4 cardinal neighbors).
- Each token near a wire endpoint sends its complement to the opposite endpoint: solid emits X, X emits diamond.

Key insight: Token shape cycles solid → X → diamond; wires route each complement to the far end.

annotation.summary: Solid 3x3 colored blocks connected to teal pipelines are split into hollow cross (stays) and solid four-star (moves to pipeline's other end); incomplete shapes at pipeline ends are completed with their counterpart.
annotation.src: solid 3x3 colored block at one end of a teal pipeline s
annotation.dst: the other end of the same teal pipeline d
annotation.path: follow teal pipeline from s to reach opposite endpoint d
annotation.transform: split s into hollow cross (center + 4 cardinal neighbors) staying at original position, and solid four-star (4 diagonal corners) moving to d
annotation.src2: hollow cross or solid four-star already at one end of teal pipeline s
annotation.dst2: the other end of the same teal pipeline d
annotation.path2: follow teal pipeline from s to reach opposite endpoint d
annotation.transform2: place the complementary shape (four-star if cross exists, cross if four-star exists) at d with same color as s

references.docstring:
Complete partial paths inside a framed rectangle by projecting external color traces inward.

Input structure:
- bg, a 1px rectangular frame (border color) with uniform interior fill.
- Colored components outside the frame touching its edges.

Rule:
- Output = the frame's interior, filled with the fill color.
- Map each outside component's frame-touch points into interior coordinates.
- Monochrome components become solid Manhattan stripes between mapped endpoints.
- Two-color components become alternating-color Manhattan paths.

Key insight: Endpoint colors of two-color traces anchor the alternating phase deterministically.

annotation.src: touch point s on closed rectangular frame where an open rectangular frame touches it
annotation.dst: connect to another touch point d on closed rectangular frame where an open rectangular frame touches it
annotation.path: path to complete the open rectangular frame
annotation.trajectory: same color and pattern as the open rectangular frame
annotation.grid_shape: crop to only retain inner area of the closed rectangular frame

references.docstring:
Add red outlines around objects, and mark enclosed holes inside hollow objects.

Input structure:
- A mostly uniform background contains one or more 4-connected foreground objects.
- Some objects may enclose 4-connected background holes inside their bbox.

Rule:
- For every foreground component, draw a one-cell 8-neighborhood outline in red (2).
- If a component has enclosed background holes, recolor the component to teal (8).
- Fill those enclosed holes with magenta (6) before drawing the outline.

Key insight: Holes are treated as part of the object for outlining, while only objects
that actually enclose holes get the teal/magenta interior recoloring.

annotation.src: blue 4-connected objects s on the background; some s enclose background holes
annotation.transform: draw a one-cell 8-neighborhood red outline around each s; if s has enclosed holes, recolor s to teal and recolor the holes to magenta before outlining

references.docstring:
Use local source-target-pattern examples to replace matching source pixels.

Input structure:
- Black background with isolated colored pixels and teal (8) pattern components.
- A rule example is a 4-neighbor colored pair source->target whose continued
  direction reaches an anchor touching a teal pattern component.

Rule:
- For each rule example, copy that teal component onto every other pixel of
  source.color, recoloring the copied component to target.color.
- Translation maps the rule anchor onto the source pixel being replaced.
- Remove teal components and all pixels used by rule examples.

Key insight: The two adjacent colored pixels define the color substitution and
the anchor point; the nearby teal component is the stencil that gets recolored.

annotation.src: colored source pixels s not part of a local rule example
annotation.dst: local rule examples d: adjacent source-color -> target-color pixel pair followed by a nearby teal stencil
annotation.match_cond: s.color == d.source_color
annotation.transform: replace each s by a translated copy of d.teal_stencil recolored to d.target_color; d.anchor aligns to s; remove teal stencils and rule-example pixels

references.docstring:
Recolor a cropped template and repeat it according to a component-count stencil.

Input structure:
- Solid blue (1) separator rows or columns split the grid into four sections.
- Section 1 is a black-background shape template; section 2 is a component-count stencil.
- Sections 3 and 4 are solid color swatches for output foreground and background.

Rule:
- Crop section 1 to the bbox of its non-black pixels and recolor it with the two swatches.
- Count 4-connected non-black components in section 2.
- Repeat the recolored crop that many times, inserting one background-colored row/column between copies.

Key insight: The second section encodes only the repeat count; the output orientation
is inherited from whether the input separators are columns or rows.

annotation.src: shape template in section 1, component-count stencil in section 2, and two solid color swatches in sections 3-4
annotation.transform: crop the section-1 template to its non-bg bbox, recolor template pixels with section-3 color and bg pixels with section-4 color, then repeat the crop once per 4-connected component in section 2 with a section-4-colored separator row/col between copies
annotation.grid_shape: horizontal or vertical strip determined by separator orientation

tags: condition:计数决定重复次数, count_determines_repetition

references.docstring:
Replicate a motif across quadrants with scaling and reflection keyed to red anchor blocks.

Input structure:
- Grid divided into four quadrants by a full-row and full-column divider of a single non-bg color.
- Each quadrant contains a red (2) square anchor block of varying size.
- The top-left quadrant also has a colored motif attached to its red anchor.

Rule:
- Use the top-left quadrant's motif as the source pattern.
- For each other quadrant, scale the motif by the ratio of that quadrant's red block size to the source red block size.
- Reflect horizontally for right-side quadrants, vertically for bottom quadrants (both for bottom-right).
- Align the scaled/reflected motif so its red region overlaps the target anchor, then stamp non-bg pixels.

Key insight: Red block size encodes the scale factor; quadrant position encodes the reflection axes.

annotation.summary: Copy the pattern adjacent to the red anchor block in the top-left quadrant to other quadrants, scaling and reflecting based on the relative size and position of matching red anchor blocks.
annotation.src: colored pixels adjacent to the red anchor block in top-left quadrant s
annotation.dst: positions adjacent to red anchor blocks in other quadrants d
annotation.match_cond: s.anchor_color == d.anchor_color (both red); scale_factor = d.red_block.size / s.red_block.size; reflection determined by quadrant relationship
annotation.trajectory: keep source
annotation.transform: scale(s, factor=d.red_block.size/src_red_block.size) and reflect(s, axis=quadrant_relative_axis)
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: identify red anchor blocks in each quadrant; Step 2: compute scale factor from red block size ratios; Step 3: determine reflection axis from quadrant positions (horizontal for left-right, vertical for top-bottom); Step 4: copy scaled and reflected pattern to each target quadrant anchored at its red block

references.docstring:
Move bordered 5×5 squares to their designated grid edges by border color.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color.
- Azure (8) and red (2) bordered 5×5 squares with colored interiors, scattered across the grid.

Rule:
- Azure squares → left edge (col 0); red squares → right edge (col W−5).
- Each square keeps its original row.
- Process azure left-to-right, red right-to-left (nearest-to-edge first).
- If a square's rows overlap an already-placed edge square, place it one square-width inward instead.

Key insight: Near-edge-first ordering plus row-overlap determines which square sits at the edge vs. the second column.

annotation.src: teal frames with colored inner
annotation.dst: stack on left edge
annotation.src2: red frames with colored inner
annotation.multi_step: stack teal frames from left to right and red frames from right to left

references.docstring:
Scale a minority cell's inner pattern up to the cell-grid level, completing a fractal overlay.

Input structure:
- Grid divided into NxN cells by separator lines of a single color.
- Most cells share an identical interior pattern (majority); a few have a distinct pattern (minority).

Rule:
- Extract the inner pixel pattern from the minority cell.
- Treat each pixel as a cell-sized stamp: active pixels → minority pattern, inactive → majority pattern.
- Position this scaled-up pattern on the cell grid so existing minority cells align with active pixels.
- Fill in all remaining active positions with the minority pattern.

Key insight: The minority cell's interior is a miniature blueprint of where minority cells should appear at the grid scale — fractal self-similarity.

annotation.summary: Find the unique cell unit with a different inner pattern, scale up that pattern fractally, and overlay it at matching cell unit positions.
annotation.src: the unique 3x3 cell unit with a different inner color pattern s
annotation.dst: cell unit positions in the grid where the scaled pattern overlays d
annotation.match_cond: s.inner_pattern scaled up where each pixel becomes a cell unit, positioned so s overlaps with some existing cell units of same pattern type
annotation.transform: scale s.inner_pattern by cell_unit_size, place at d, non-overlapping cells overwrite original grid
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: identify repeating 3x3 cell units forming the grid pattern; Step 2: find the unique cell unit with a different inner pattern; Step 3: extract the inner pixel pattern of the unique unit; Step 4: scale pattern up so each pixel maps to one cell unit; Step 5: position scaled pattern so it aligns with the unique unit location; Step 6: overlay scaled pattern, non-matching cells overwrite background
annotation.notes: Fractal self-similarity approach - the unique anomalous cell unit contains a miniature pattern that gets scaled up to cell-unit level and overlaid on the grid

references.docstring:
Fill the region enclosed by a wall sprite and radiate color outward through its opening.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color. Wall = most frequent non-bg color, forming a partial enclosure (e.g. U-shape).
- A fill-color pixel sits inside the enclosed area. Other non-bg pixels may act as obstacles.
Rule:
- Flood-fill the enclosed area with the fill color, radiating outward through the wall's open end.
- Obstacles cast "shadows" along the radiate direction, blocking fill behind them.

Key insight: The wall endpoints define the opening direction; fill radiates outward through it, and obstacles block propagation along that same axis.

annotation.summary: A pixel inside a half-surrounded area fills and radiates outward along the border opening, while isolated pixels move to grid edge in the radiate direction, leaving background trail
annotation.src: innermost connected same-color pixel s inside the half-surrounded inner area of a sprite
annotation.path: fill the surrounded area and radiate along the surrounded border opening
annotation.notes: In the second transformation, the sprite s acts as an obstacle blocking the path of s2
annotation.src2: isolated color pixel s2 away from the surrounded area bottleneck
annotation.path2: straight line to the edge of the grid, same as the radiate direction

references.docstring:
Scale up a monochrome control sprite by stamping a polychrome tile at each filled pixel.

Input structure:
- bg = background color.
- Two foreground objects (8-connected): a monochrome rectangular sprite with bg holes (control), and a polychrome square tile (block).

Rule:
- For each cell in the control sprite's bbox: if filled, stamp a copy of the block tile; if bg, leave a tile-sized bg region.
- Output grid dimensions are (control_h × tile_h) by (control_w × tile_w).

Key insight: The control sprite acts as a binary mask that gets "pixel-scaled" by the tile — each pixel expands to a full tile copy or empty space.

annotation.src: monochrome sprite
annotation.transform: enlarge each pixel into the polychrome square
annotation.grid_shape: tight crop to retain only the enlarged sprite

references.docstring:
Complete a grid of colored blocks to match a minimap legend in the top-left corner.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color.
- Top-left corner: a small sprite of single colored pixels forming a minimap pattern on a regular lattice.
- Main area: uniformly colored square blocks (NxN) arranged on a regular grid; some positions are empty (bg).

Rule:
- The legend pixels define a color pattern; each pixel's lattice position maps to a block position in the main grid via a fixed scale factor and offset.
- Existing colored blocks confirm the scale/offset alignment.
- For every legend pixel whose corresponding grid position is empty, place a new block of that color.

Key insight: The top-left pixel pattern is a scaled-down minimap of the block layout; the mapping is inferred from blocks already present.

annotation.summary: A small legend sprite in the top-left corner defines a pattern that maps to existing colored blocks in the grid; missing pixels from the legend are then placed at corresponding scaled positions.
annotation.src: pixels in top-left legend sprite s that are not yet represented in the main grid
annotation.dst: scaled grid positions d corresponding to legend pixel positions
annotation.match_cond: s.legend_position maps to d.grid_position via scale factor derived from existing colored blocks alignment
annotation.trajectory: keep source
annotation.symbol_instructions: top-left pixel pattern serves as minimap legend defining full pattern to be placed at scaled positions in grid
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: identify top-left legend sprite (small colored pattern); Step 2: locate existing colored blocks in main grid that match some legend pixels; Step 3: compute scale factor and offset from legend to grid; Step 4: for each legend pixel not yet in grid, place scaled block at computed position

references.docstring:
Swap every sprite to the opposite prototype while preserving scale and position.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color. Two distinct small sprite patterns (prototypes) appear at various scales.
- Each sprite instance is a scaled copy of one of the two prototypes, placed on the grid.

Rule:
- Identify the two prototype patterns from the smallest-area sprites.
- For each sprite, determine which prototype it matches and its integer scale factor.
- Replace it with the other prototype at the same scale, aligned by an internal anchor region (color-1 pixels).

Key insight: Every sprite toggles to the alternate prototype; the anchor sub-region inside each sprite pins the alignment so swapped sprites land in the correct position regardless of scale.

annotation.summary: Sprites are classified into two groups by their color pattern, then the patterns are swapped between groups while preserving each sprite's scale and maximizing position overlap.
annotation.src: polychrome sprites with distinct color combinations s
annotation.dst: matched sprite from opposite pattern group d
annotation.match_cond: s.pattern_group != d.pattern_group && s.scale == d.scale && maximize(s.position_overlap_with(d.position))
annotation.transform: swap s.color_pattern with d.color_pattern while preserving s.scale
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: identify all non-background sprites; Step 2: classify sprites into two groups by color pattern (e.g., group A has teal/green, group B has red/green); Step 3: swap color patterns between matched pairs while keeping positions with maximum overlap, and same scale

references.docstring:
Extend a green path from one grid edge to the opposite, routing around red bars at a distance dictated by their blue pixel count.

Input structure:
- bg = azure (8). Red/blue bars (color 2/1) act as obstacles.
- A single green (3) pixel sits on a grid border — the path start.

Rule:
- Each bar's keep-out radius equals its number of blue pixels; the path must stay farther than that from every bar cell.
- The green pixel extends inward toward the opposite edge, turning at right angles to navigate around forbidden zones.
- After the path is drawn, all blue pixels become red.

Key insight: Blue pixels on a bar encode its danger radius — more blue means a wider no-go zone the path must respect.

annotation.summary: Green pixel on grid edge extends toward red bars while maintaining minimum distance from each red bar determined by the count of blue pixels on that bar, then blue pixels turn red.
annotation.src: green pixel on grid edge s
annotation.dst: traverse past all red bars d
annotation.path: extend from edge toward red bars, turning at right angles to navigate around obstacles
annotation.trajectory: paint green along path, maintaining distance > blue_pixel_count from each red bar
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: count blue pixels on each red bar to determine minimum distance; Step 2: extend green path from edge maintaining distance from red bars; Step 3: convert all blue pixels to red
annotation.src2: blue pixels on red bars s

tags: relation:像素计数编码半径, pixel_count_encodes_radius

references.docstring:
Assemble scattered jigsaw sprites around a central yellow anchor by pairing red connector pixels.

Input structure:
- bg = black (0). Several colored sprites scattered on the grid.
- One anchor sprite contains a 3×3 yellow (4) block.
- Each sprite has red (2) connector pixels along its edges.

Rule:
- The anchor stays in place; remaining sprites attach one at a time.
- Each sprite is translated so that one of its red pixels overlaps an unpaired red pixel on the growing assembly.
- Every red connector must pair with exactly one other, forming a complete joined structure.

Key insight: Red pixels act as jigsaw pegs — each must match exactly one counterpart, and the assembly order is determined by which unpaired connectors remain.

annotation.summary: Scattered sprites with red connector pixels are assembled around a central yellow block by matching red connectors to form a connected structure.
annotation.src: scattered colored sprites with red connector pixels s
annotation.dst: attach to the central yellow block or to already-attached sprites d
annotation.match_cond: s.red_pixel aligns with d.red_pixel to form connection
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: identify central yellow block as anchor; Step 2: find sprite with red pixel that can connect to anchor's red pixel; Step 3: attach sprite by aligning red connectors; Step 4: repeat until all sprites connected

references.docstring:
Transfer center colors between bordered sprites matched by color, keeping only path-connected ones.

Input structure:
- bg, grey (5) path network, and several small "bordered sprites" each having a border color and a single center pixel of a different color.
- Grey path forms a one-stroke trail under 8-connectivity; its start/end cells touch exactly two destination sprites via ports.

Rule:
- Destination sprites are determined by the grey trail's two endpoints.
- For each destination, find the source sprite whose border color equals the destination's center color.
- Replace the destination's center pixel with the source's center color.
- Delete all non-destination sprites; grey paths and destinations remain.

Key insight: Center color of each destination acts as a lookup key into the border colors of other sprites, enabling indirect color transfer.

annotation.summary: Find sprites connected to grey path endpoints, match source sprites by border color to destination center color, transfer source center color to destination center, then delete unconnected sprites.
annotation.src: colored bordered sprites s (sprites with center color and border color)
annotation.dst: colored bordered sprites d connected to grey path endpoints (path endpoint must connect to sprite's center position)
annotation.match_cond: s.border_color == d.center_color
annotation.transform: s.center_color -> d.center_color
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: identify grey connected path and sprites at path endpoints (d); Step 2: for each d, find s where s.border_color == d.center_color; Step 3: copy s.center_color to d.center; Step 4: delete all sprites not connected to grey path
annotation.src2: all sprites not connected to grey path

references.docstring:
Delete connected components whose colors match a legend swatch.

Input structure:
- Background (bg) fills most of the grid.
- Top-left corner: a small square legend region bordered on its bottom and right edges by a single color; the interior holds a set of "target" colors.
- Elsewhere: multicolored objects (4-connected components) on the bg.

Rule:
- Read the target color set from inside the legend border.
- For each connected component, check whether it contains **all** target colors.
- Erase (fill with bg) every component that does; leave all others unchanged.
- Output grid is the same size.

Key insight: The legend acts as a filter specification — only components carrying the full color palette shown in the legend are removed.

annotation.summary: Delete all connected components that contain all the colors present in the top-left legend region.
annotation.src: connected components containing all legend colors s
annotation.match_cond: s.colors contains all colors from legend region (green-bordered area in top-left corner)
annotation.transform: delete(s)
annotation.symbol_instructions: legend in top-left green-bordered region defines target color set
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: identify legend colors from top-left corner; Step 2: find all connected components; Step 3: delete components that contain ALL legend colors

references.docstring:
Look up query glyphs in a reference table and mark whether they form a line.

Input structure:
- Teal background with two full-width pink separator rows.
- Above the first separator is a query row of 5x5 glyph cells.
- Between separators is a reference table of the same 5x5 cells; a glyph is
  identified by both its color and its 3x3 shape.

Rule:
- Green-fill the background inside every table cell whose glyph exactly
  appears in the query row.
- If the matched table cells form one complete row or one complete column,
  also green-fill the query band and the bottom verdict band.
- Otherwise leave the query band unchanged and fill the bottom verdict band red.

Key insight: The bottom color is not a count; it is the yes/no answer to
whether the queried glyphs align as a full row or column in the table.

annotation.src: query glyph cells s above the first separator row
annotation.dst: reference table glyph cells d between the separator rows
annotation.match_cond: s and d have the same color and same 3x3 glyph shape within their 5x5 cell
annotation.transform: green-fill the background inside each matched d cell; if all query glyphs match cells forming one complete table row or column, also green-fill the query band and bottom verdict band, otherwise fill only the bottom verdict band red

references.docstring:
Grow four clockwise spiral wall paths from the tips of a teal cross.

Input structure:
- bg = 0 (black). A single teal (8) cross centered in the grid.

Rule:
- Each arm tip launches a "turtle" heading 90° right of its outward direction.
- Movement priority: turn right > go straight > turn left (left only if not on border).
- Normal step = 2 cells; step right after a turn = 1 cell.
- Each new cell must have a 1-cell orthogonal gap from all existing walls except the predecessor.

Key insight: The right-turn preference plus alternating 2/1 step lengths creates self-avoiding spirals that tile the grid with uniform spacing.

annotation.summary: Four endpoints of a teal cross emit same-colored spiral trajectories clockwise, filling the grid like a kaleidoscope with one-pixel spacing between trails.
annotation.src: four endpoint pixels of the teal cross s
annotation.path: each endpoint emits ray clockwise spiraling inward/outward, turning 90 degrees at boundaries or when spacing constraint requires, with initial backward step before proceeding
annotation.trajectory: paint s.color continuously with one-pixel gap between adjacent spiral arms

references.docstring:
Expand a 3x3 block motif into a 5x5 block motif around its missing center.

Input structure:
- Teal background surrounds one 9x9 foreground motif.
- The motif is a 3x3 array of 3x3 blocks; the middle block is empty teal.
- Colored pixels immediately around the empty middle block encode the border
  of the missing center block.

Rule:
- Keep the original 9x9 motif in place.
- Copy each of the eight surrounding 3x3 blocks to the opposite outer slot
  of the implied 5x5 block grid, without rotating it.
- Fill the center block from the eight pixels around the hole; its center is
  the motif's majority foreground color.

Key insight: The visible 9x9 motif is the middle of a larger periodic
block-level pattern, and the empty center is reconstructed from its immediate
inner boundary.

annotation.src: the visible 9x9 motif: a 3x3 array of 3x3 blocks with the center block missing
annotation.dst: the implied outer slots of a 5x5 block grid around the same center
annotation.transform: copy each non-center 3x3 block to the opposite outer slot without rotation; reconstruct the missing center block from the eight immediate boundary pixels around the hole, using the motif majority foreground color for the center pixel

references.docstring:
Connect same-color diagonal pixel pairs, then emit perpendicular rays from differently-colored pixels on those diagonals.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color. Line color (e.g. blue) has pixel pairs aligned on shared diagonals. Trigger color (e.g. magenta) pixels sit along those diagonals.

Rule:
- Draw diagonal lines connecting each pair of same-color aligned pixels.
- Where the diagonal crosses a trigger pixel, emit perpendicular diagonal rays (in the trigger's color) extending to the grid boundary.
- Moved maroons are erased (replaced with floor color).

Key insight: Trigger pixels act as beam-splitters — the perpendicular rays rotate 90° from the connecting diagonal's orientation.

annotation.summary: Connect blue pixels diagonally, and if the diagonal line passes through a magenta pixel, extend perpendicular diagonal lines from that magenta pixel.
annotation.src: pair of blue pixels s
annotation.path: diagonal line connecting s.pixel1 to s.pixel2
annotation.trajectory: paint blue along diagonal path between the two blue pixels
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: draw diagonal line connecting blue pixels; Step 2: for each magenta pixel on the diagonal, draw perpendicular diagonal lines extending to grid boundaries
annotation.src2: magenta pixels that lie on the blue diagonal line s
annotation.path2: perpendicular diagonal directions (90 degree rotation from original diagonal) from s until grid boundary
annotation.trajectory2: paint magenta along both perpendicular diagonal directions

references.docstring:
Fill hollow sprites' interiors using a color-palette legend on the grid edge.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color. Several hollow sprites with distinct border colors.
- A small 2×N or N×2 palette block sits on one grid edge; one row/column lists border colors, the other lists corresponding fill colors.

Rule:
- Locate the palette legend on a grid edge and read it as a border→fill color mapping.
- Find enclosed bg regions (holes) inside sprites that don't touch the grid boundary.
- For each hole, identify the most common adjacent border color, look it up in the palette, and fill the hole with the mapped fill color.

Key insight: The palette's edge position and orientation determine reading direction; border colors in the palette uniquely key into fill colors.

annotation.summary: Use a color palette legend on the grid edge to fill sprites' interiors based on their border color mapping.
annotation.src: hollow sprites with colored borders s
annotation.dst: interior of same sprite d
annotation.match_cond: d.fill_color == palette_lookup(s.border_color)
annotation.transform: fill d with palette[s.border_color]
annotation.symbol_instructions: palette is 2xN or Nx2 block on grid edge; read direction based on edge position: top edge reads top-to-bottom, bottom edge reads bottom-to-top, left edge reads left-to-right; first row/column is border color, second is fill color
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: locate 2xN or Nx2 palette legend on grid edge; Step 2: build color mapping (border -> fill) based on reading direction; Step 3: for each hollow sprite, lookup border color in palette and fill interior with corresponding fill color
annotation.notes: The challenge is correctly reading the palette legend based on its edge position and orientation

references.docstring:
Move the closest reachable maroon pixels into the 3×3 block around the unique red center.

Input structure:
- bg = orange floor, magenta walls, scattered maroon (9) pixels.
- A unique red (2) pixel marks the center of a 3×3 destination block.

Rule:
- Maroon pixels connected to the destination through floor/maroon cells (not blocked by walls) are candidates.
- Rank candidates by distance to the destination; the closest ones fill the block in row-major order.
- Moved maroons are erased (replaced with floor color).

Key insight: Wall barriers restrict connectivity — only maroon pixels reachable via flood-fill through the floor qualify, so proximity alone isn't enough.

annotation.summary: Maroon pixels reachable through orange background from the green square with red center are collected and fill the green square from top-left, sorted by distance.

annotation.dst: green square with red center d
annotation.match_cond: s is connected to d via orange pixels (not blocked by magenta walls)
annotation.path: collect s pixels sorted by distance to d, fill d.interior from top-left in row-major order
annotation.trajectory: s disappears from original position, appears at d.interior positions

references.docstring:
Turn black dents in two colored regions into marked opposite-color patches.

Input structure:
- Black background with two large foreground colors.
- The large regions contain small black dents and a few one-cell color specks
  or protrusions along region boundaries.

Rule:
- Locally clean the two foreground regions: isolated specks become black, and
  one-cell protrusions surrounded by the other region take that region's color.
- Each original black dent whose cleaned 3x3 neighborhood is mostly one
  foreground color becomes the center of a 3x3 patch in the opposite color.
- The dent center itself is recolored teal (8).

Key insight: The teal pixels mark the original black defects; the surrounding
3x3 patch uses the other foreground color, after first removing boundary noise.

annotation.src: black dents inside two large foreground-color regions, with possible one-cell foreground specks or boundary protrusions
annotation.transform: first locally clean the foreground regions by removing isolated specks and recoloring one-cell protrusions to the surrounding region color; then each original black dent whose cleaned 3x3 neighborhood is mostly one foreground color becomes a 3x3 patch of the other foreground color with the dent center recolored teal

references.docstring:
Expand each colored control pixel into its corresponding fixed 4x4 glyph.

Input structure:
- Black background with single-pixel markers in colors 2, 3, 5, and/or 8.
- Some inputs also show a sample 4x4 glyph in the output color, with a same-rule marker just below-right of the sample.

Rule:
- Replace each marker color by its learned 4x4 glyph: 2->yellow frame, 3->blue ring, 5->pink diagonal blocks, 8->orange X.
- Paint each glyph with its top-left corner at the marker pixel, clipping at the grid boundary.
- Remove the sample glyphs and skip their below-right label markers.

Key insight:
- The colored pixels are control pixels for a fixed glyph alphabet; non-control sample glyphs are only legend entries, not preserved scene objects.

annotation.src: single-pixel markers in the glyph alphabet colors
annotation.transform: replace each marker by its fixed 4x4 glyph, clipped at grid edge; sample glyphs and their below-right labels disappear

references.docstring:
Emit diagonal beams from framed 2x2 blocks through frame gaps; beams interact on collision.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color. Wall color (e.g. green) forms 4x4 frames around 2x2 monochrome blocks.
- Each frame has one or more gap pixels where the wall is missing.

Rule:
- Each gap emits a beam of the inner block's color, traveling diagonally outward (direction set by gap position relative to the block).
- Beams paint every cell they cross until they hit the grid edge or collide.
- 90° collision: both beams turn 45° toward their bisector direction; the intersection cell is left blank (1-pixel gap).
- 45° collision: beams merge into a zigzag (alternating cardinal + diagonal steps) with no gap at the meeting point.

Key insight: Two distinct collision rules — 90° produces a gap and single-pixel diagonal lines; 45° produces no gap and thicker zigzag bands.

annotation.summary: Inner colored pixels inside green frames emit outward through gaps in the green border, traveling diagonally until hitting grid boundary or another path, with collision rules determining trajectory changes.
annotation.src: non-green colored pixels inside green frames s
annotation.path: emit diagonally outward from gap in green frame, direction determined by gap position relative to s; continue until grid boundary or collision with another path
annotation.trajectory: paint s.color along entire diagonal path; when two paths collide at 90 degrees, both turn 45 degrees with one pixel gap at intersection and form diagonal line using single pixels; when paths meet at 45 degrees, paths merge without gap and both turn 22.5 degrees forming line using 2x2 pixel blocks
annotation.notes: Critical collision rule: for 90-degree collisions with 45-degree turns, there is a one-pixel gap at intersection and paths are drawn as single diagonal pixels; for 45-degree collisions with 22.5-degree turns, there is no gap and paths are drawn as 2x2 pixel blocks

references.docstring:
Recolor grey shapes by matching their hole count to a color legend.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color; grey (5) sprites scattered across the grid.
- Colored legend shapes (non-bg, non-grey, at least 2×2, not touching the outer border) near grid edge,
  each with a distinct number of enclosed holes.

Rule:
- Each colored legend shape defines a mapping: hole count → color.
- For every grey sprite, count its holes (enclosed bg regions not touching the sprite's bounding-box border).
- Recolor the grey sprite to the matching legend color; erase grey distractors with unlisted hole counts.

Key insight: Shape identity is encoded by topology (number of holes), not geometry or size.

annotation.summary: Grey sprites in the grid are recolored based on matching their hole count to legend shapes, where each legend shape has a specific color and hole count.
annotation.src: grey sprites scattered in the grid s
annotation.dst: colored legend shapes in the top-left corner d
annotation.match_cond: s.hole_count == d.hole_count
annotation.transform: s.color = d.color
annotation.symbol_instructions: legend shapes (colored sprites at grid edge) define color assignment: count holes in each legend shape; grey sprites with same hole count get recolored to that legend's color
annotation.notes: The difficulty lies in counting holes in each shape

references.docstring:
Align parallel colored line segments so they all share the same start and end positions as a reference line.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color.
- Several parallel line segments (diagonal, horizontal, or vertical), each a different color, running in the same direction but starting/ending at different positions.

Rule:
- Detect the dominant direction shared by all segments.
- Pick the median segment (by perpendicular offset) as the reference.
- Shift every segment along the shared direction so its start aligns with the reference's start, then trim or extend it to match the reference's length.
- Grid size stays the same; isolated single pixels are untouched.

Key insight: The reference is the median line, not the longest; all segments are snapped to its extent regardless of their original length.

annotation.summary: Parallel diagonal lines of different colors are aligned at both ends to match the second-longest line's extent.
annotation.src: diagonal lines of different colors s
annotation.dst: aligned position matching the second-longest line's endpoints d
annotation.match_cond: s.endpoints align with d.endpoints where d is the line with second-longest length
annotation.transform: extend or trim s so both endpoints align with the reference line's extent
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: identify all diagonal lines by color; Step 2: calculate each line's length; Step 3: find the second-longest line as reference; Step 4: align all other lines' endpoints to match the reference line's start and end positions

references.docstring:
Assemble scattered colored fragments into a left-right symmetric rectangle, jigsaw-style.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color; remaining colors form small sprite fragments.
- Optional roles: 4 singleton pixels of one color mark corners; horizontal bars mark top/bottom edges; paired vertical lines mark left/right edges.

Rule:
- Collect all non-bg connected components as jigsaw pieces.
- Determine output rectangle dimensions from total piece area.
- Pack pieces into the rectangle so it is exactly mirror-symmetric (left-right) and same-color pieces never 4-touch.

Key insight: Left-right symmetry plus the no-same-color-touching constraint make the assembly unique; corner/edge markers anchor it when present.

annotation.summary: Assemble scattered pixels and sprites into a complete composite image by matching edges without rotation.
annotation.src: scattered non-background pixels and sprite fragments s
annotation.dst: assembled rectangular composite shape d
annotation.match_cond: s.edge.position aligns with d.adjacent_piece.edge to form continuous rectangular shape
annotation.grid_shape: tight crop
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: identify all non-background colored fragments; Step 2: assemble fragments by matching their edges to form complete jigsaw-like composition; Step 3: output tight crop of assembled result
annotation.notes: output has exact left-right mirror symmetry; same-color pieces must not 4-touch each other

references.docstring:
Emit four teal beams from a square, turning at colored obstacles per a legend.

Input structure:
- Top band: grey (5) legend with colored vertical bars in cells; bar position (left or right) encodes turn direction.
- Below: main grid with bg, a solid teal (8) square, and colored obstacle blocks.

Rule:
- Remove the legend from the output.
- From the teal square, shoot a beam in each cardinal direction (as a sliding copy of the square).
- Each beam paints teal over bg cells as it moves.
- On hitting an obstacle of color C, consult the legend: bar on left → turn counterclockwise, bar on right → turn clockwise. Continue in the new direction.
- Beams stop at grid edges.

Key insight: The legend's bar position (left vs right within its cell) is the encoding for turn direction at each obstacle color.

annotation.summary: Isolated teal square emits lines in four directions, turning on obstacle contact based on legend color bar position.
annotation.src: isolated teal square s
annotation.path: extend in 4 cardinal directions; on hitting obstacle, turn counterclockwise if legend shows same-color bar on left, clockwise if on right
annotation.trajectory: paint teal along path until obstacle or grid edge
annotation.symbol_instructions: legend entries: obstacle_color with bar on left → counterclockwise turn; bar on right → clockwise turn
annotation.grid_shape: tight crop
annotation.src2: grey legend region at top s

references.docstring:
Stamp recolored sprites into a framed region using placeholder positions and a color legend.

Input structure:
- bg background, a rectangular single-color frame, colored placeholder cells inside the frame.
- Outside the frame: sprite shapes (one per placeholder color) and a small legend mapping each placeholder color to an output color.

Rule:
- Find the frame and its interior placeholders.
- For each placeholder color, locate the matching-color sprite outside the frame.
- Stamp each sprite at the placeholder's position inside the frame.
- Recolor every stamped sprite to the output color defined by the legend.

Key insight: The legend pairs (overlapping two-color glyphs outside the frame) dictate the final recoloring — placeholder color selects the shape, legend maps it to the output color.

annotation.summary: Replace colored cells inside grey frame with sprites from outside matching by color, then recolor sprites according to shape-color legend in top-left corner.

annotation.dst: single colored pixels inside the grey frame d
annotation.match_cond: s.color == d.color
annotation.transform: replace d with s.shape
annotation.symbol_instructions: top-left legend maps shape patterns to output colors; each unique shape gets recolored to its legend-defined color
annotation.grid_shape: grey frame region

annotation.src2: placed sprites inside the frame with various shapes s2
annotation.dst2: legend entries in top-left corner showing shape-color pairs d2

references.docstring:
Decode the colored 3x3 contour motif into a 16x16 periodic lattice with the motif stamped in maroon at the center.

Input structure:
- The grid is 6x6 with orange background and one non-orange color.
- The non-orange pixels have a tight 3x3 bbox containing one contour glyph.
- The glyph is one of the task's period-3 contour forms: plus, H, X, or four corners.

Rule:
- Decode the 3x3 glyph into the period-3 orange phase tile.
- Fill a black 16x16 canvas by repeating that orange phase tile.
- Tile the original 3x3 glyph 2x2 and recolor its true pixels to maroon in the centered 6x6 region.

Key insight:
- The colored object is not copied at its input location; it is a small contour code whose phase tells where orange appears in the repeated lattice.

annotation.src: colored 3x3 contour glyph in the orange 6x6 grid
annotation.dst: 16x16 black canvas with a period-3 orange lattice and centered 6x6 motif region
annotation.transform: decode the glyph into the orange phase tile; repeat that tile over the canvas; tile the glyph 2x2 at the center and recolor its foreground pixels maroon

references.docstring:
Assemble scattered jigsaw pieces into a rectangle, recoloring each by a legend sprite's color map.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color.
- Several monochrome non-bg sprites (the "pieces"), scattered across the grid.
- One sprite is the legend: it contains a multi-color k×k patch (typically 2×2) encoding output colors.

Rule:
- Tile all pieces (rotations/reflections allowed) into a tight rectangle with no gaps.
- The legend's k×k color patch defines a spatial color map over the rectangle.
- Each piece is recolored to the legend-map color corresponding to its position in the assembled rectangle.

Key insight: The legend piece doubles as both a jigsaw piece and a color key — its internal k×k palette assigns colors by spatial quadrant.

annotation.summary: Assemble scattered sprites into a composite shape using a legend sprite that specifies colors for each component position.
annotation.src: monochrome sprites scattered in the grid s
annotation.dst: assemble into composite shape matching the legend sprite's silhouette d
annotation.match_cond: s.shape matches d.region.shape (d is always in top-left, final assembly forms rectangle)
annotation.transform: s.color = legend[s.position_in_composite].color
annotation.symbol_instructions: legend sprite contains 2x2 colored pixels where each pixel's position (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right) maps to corresponding sprite's recolor in final assembly
annotation.grid_shape: tight crop
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: identify legend sprite (contains multi-color 2x2 pattern); Step 2: identify other monochrome sprites with same shape structure; Step 3: assemble sprites into composite matching legend silhouette; Step 4: recolor each assembled region based on legend position mapping

references.docstring:
Count the two upper quadrant control regions to size an output made from the lower quadrant pattern.

Input structure:
- The grid is an even square split into four equal quadrants.
- Black is the background.
- The upper-left and upper-right quadrants are control regions.
- The lower-left quadrant is a color source tile; the lower-right quadrant is either a stencil tile or empty.

Rule:
- Output height is the number of non-background pixels in the upper-left quadrant.
- Output width is the number of non-background pixels in the upper-right quadrant.
- If the lower-right stencil has foreground pixels, tile it over the output; each stencil background pixel is filled from the lower-left quadrant cell at the corresponding coarse tile position.
- If the lower-right stencil is empty, tile the lower-left quadrant directly over the output.

Key insight:
- The top quadrants specify only dimensions, while the bottom quadrants specify a two-level repeated pattern: a fine stencil and coarse fill colors.

annotation.src: lower-left color source tile and lower-right stencil tile
annotation.dst: output rectangle sized by foreground counts in the upper-left and upper-right control quadrants
annotation.transform: tile the lower-right stencil; replace each stencil background pixel with the corresponding coarse lower-left color, or tile the lower-left region directly when the stencil is empty
annotation.grid_shape: height = count(upper-left foreground), width = count(upper-right foreground)

references.docstring:
Repair a one-cell-thick colored line network by replacing singleton markers, filling short orthogonal gaps, and redirecting yellow-marked arms to the edge.

Input structure:
- A rectangular grid with a dominant background.
- Line colors form one-cell-thick horizontal/vertical stroke fragments.
- Marker colors are exactly those whose 4-connected components are all singleton pixels.
- Red singleton markers are missing line cells; yellow singleton markers are directional controls next to a line endpoint.

Rule:
- Assign every marker to the nearest visible line color in row/column line-of-sight, preferring an endpoint supported along that same axis.
- For each line color, fill the gap between consecutive facing endpoints in a row or column.
- A yellow control erases the old straight arm on the far side of its endpoint and paints the same color from that endpoint through the control pixel to the grid edge.
- At crossings, yellow-control rays win; otherwise an original-vs-filled crossing uses the more fragmented pre-repair line color, while pure filled crossings use the lower color id.

Key insight: The singleton markers identify which sparse stroke fragments belong together; after they are colored, the intended lines are the axis-aligned gaps between facing endpoints, with yellow controls flipping one arm to the marked side.

annotation.src: one-cell-thick colored line network with singleton red/yellow marker pixels
annotation.transform: replace each marker by its assigned line color, fill facing horizontal/vertical gaps, and use yellow controls to erase the old arm and paint the same color from the endpoint through the marker to the grid edge
annotation.notes: crossings prefer yellow-control rays; otherwise original-vs-filled crossings use the more fragmented repaired line, and marker-bracketed filled gaps beat unmarked pure fills

references.docstring:
Align a central rectangle to two colored frame-edge controls via rotation/reflection.

Input structure:
- bg grid with two solid-colored border edges (distinct non-bg colors).
- A central filled rectangle with 1px colored guide edges on two sides, colors matching the frame controls.

Rule:
- Rotate/mirror the object so its guide edges face the same sides as the matching frame controls.
- Crop off the 1px guide edges from aligned sides.

Key insight: Guide-edge colors encode target frame sides; the correct dihedral transform matches both simultaneously.

annotation.src: rectangle s with two colored edges
annotation.dst: move to grid corner d
annotation.match_cond: s.edge.colors == d.colored_edges.colors (may rotate/flip)
annotation.transform: crop off guide edges after alignment
